title: Pooling mode and session-state compatibility
description: Choose a release boundary and a PostgreSQL feature. The trace shows whether the next operation can rely on the same backend session and what contract the application must adopt.

modes.label: Session pooling
modes.detail: Hold one server connection until the client disconnects.
modes.backendContinuity: Same backend for the client session

trace.label: Between operations
trace.event: Server remains pinned to the client

trace.label: Operation 2
trace.event: The same session state is visible

modes.label: Transaction pooling
modes.detail: Return the server connection after COMMIT or ROLLBACK.

trace.label: COMMIT
trace.event: Backend A is released for another client

trace.label: Transaction 2
trace.event: A different session may be assigned

modes.label: Statement pooling
modes.detail: Return the server connection after every statement.

features.label: Session SET then later query
features.detail: Run SET search_path, commit, and expect a later transaction to inherit it.

session.explanation: The client keeps one backend, so session settings remain available until disconnect.
session.alternative: Keep DISCARD ALL as the session-pool reset query before this backend is reused by another client.

transaction.explanation: The next transaction can use another backend, while the old SET value may remain on the previous backend.
transaction.alternative: Use SET LOCAL inside each explicit transaction, or use a PgBouncer-tracked startup parameter when appropriate.

statement.explanation: The setting statement and dependent query need not use the same backend.
statement.alternative: Make the operation one self-contained statement or choose a less aggressive pooling mode.

features.label: Protocol-level named prepared statement
features.detail: A driver uses PostgreSQL extended-protocol Parse, Bind, and Execute messages.

session.explanation: The prepared plan belongs to the backend pinned to this client session.
session.alternative: Test schema migration behavior and clear stale plans during controlled connection rotation.

transaction.explanation: PgBouncer can track, rename, and prepare the statement on whichever backend is assigned.
transaction.alternative: Set max_prepared_statements above zero explicitly and test the exact driver and PgBouncer versions.

statement.explanation: PgBouncer can track protocol-level prepared statements even though each statement may use another backend.
statement.alternative: The complete operation must still fit statement-pooling autocommit semantics.

features.label: SQL PREPARE and EXECUTE
features.detail: The application sends PREPARE in one command and EXECUTE in a later command.

session.explanation: Both SQL commands reach the same pinned PostgreSQL session.
session.alternative: Reset prepared state before the backend is assigned to another client.

transaction.explanation: PgBouncer's prepared-statement tracking does not rewrite SQL PREPARE, EXECUTE, or DEALLOCATE.
transaction.alternative: Use a tested driver's protocol-level prepared statements or disable server-side preparation.

statement.explanation: The later EXECUTE can reach a backend that never received PREPARE.
statement.alternative: Use protocol-level tracking with a non-zero cache or send an ordinary parameterized statement.

features.label: LISTEN for notifications
features.detail: A client expects a long-lived session to keep a notification subscription.

session.explanation: The subscription remains attached to the backend pinned to the client.
session.alternative: Use a dedicated connection and reconnect-resubscribe logic.

transaction.explanation: The listening backend returns to the pool and later notifications are not tied to the original client.
transaction.alternative: Route notification listeners through session pooling or a direct PostgreSQL connection.

statement.explanation: A statement-scoped assignment cannot preserve a notification subscription.
statement.alternative: Use a dedicated session outside the statement-pooled path.

features.label: SET LOCAL inside a transaction
features.detail: Set request-specific state and consume it before COMMIT.

session.explanation: Transaction-local state is valid and automatically disappears when the transaction ends.
session.alternative: Keep request state transaction-scoped even when session pooling is available.

transaction.explanation: Every statement in the transaction uses one assigned backend, and SET LOCAL ends at COMMIT or ROLLBACK.
transaction.alternative: Make transaction boundaries explicit and never return a connection mid-transaction.

statement.explanation: Statement pooling rejects the multi-statement transaction needed to set and later consume transaction-local state.
statement.alternative: Use transaction pooling for multi-statement units of work.

features.label: Session-level advisory lock
features.detail: Acquire a lock and expect to release it from a later transaction.

session.explanation: The same backend is retained, but disconnects and reset behavior still define lock lifetime and recovery.
session.alternative: Prefer transaction-level advisory locks when the critical section fits one transaction.

transaction.explanation: The unlock can reach another backend while the original session continues holding the lock.
transaction.alternative: Use pg_advisory_xact_lock so PostgreSQL releases the lock at transaction end.

statement.explanation: There is no stable backend session across lock and unlock statements.
statement.alternative: Move the critical section to one transaction on a transaction- or session-pooled path.
